text: SQL injection exists the moment untrusted input gets concatenated directly into a query string instead of being passed as data. In a login form built that way, submitting a username of a single quote, OR one equals one, two dashes, turns the WHERE clause into a statement that's always true and comments out the password check entirely. That's the simplest case: authentication-bypass injection.

From there, a tester works through three broader techniques. Error-based injection feeds in a lone quote and reads the database error the app leaks back — a verbose error naming a table confirms input reaches the query unsanitized. UNION-based injection appends a UNION SELECT with a matching column count to pull data from other tables into the same response. Blind injection asks yes-or-no questions indirectly, through boolean logic that changes page behavior, or a SLEEP payload that makes the response slower when the condition is true.

Parameterized queries are the real fix — the driver binds input as data, so a submitted quote can't break out of its slot. But a tester never assumes an app is safe just because it uses an ORM. The job is verifying every input path actually uses binding, including paths frameworks make easy to skip: a raw-SQL escape hatch, a sort column pulled straight from the query string, or a value stored safely once and concatenated unsafely later.

Cross-site scripting works differently — attacker input gets reflected into a response and executed by the victim's browser. Reflected XSS rides in the request and only affects whoever clicks a crafted link. Stored XSS is saved server-side, in a comment or profile field, and executes for every later viewer — far higher impact. DOM-based XSS never touches the server at all; a client-side script reads attacker-controlled data and writes it unsafely into the page.

A tester's starting payload against an authorized target is usually something inert and self-confirming, adjusted to context — an HTML attribute, a script block, and plain body text each need a different escape sequence. Confirming the alert fires proves execution; the finding documents the exact parameter, context, and whether a Content Security Policy blocked it.

Every payload here only ever runs against an explicitly in-scope target under a signed Rules of Engagement — and a stored XSS payload gets cleaned up immediately after confirmation, since leaving one sitting in a client's production data would itself be a problem the engagement caused. Next lesson, we move from injection into authentication and session flaws: predictable tokens, sessions that outlive a logout, and password reset flows that quietly hand over an account.
